sources.title: How to Care for Your Aquarium Fish During a Power Outage
Air Stones: The Secret Weapon Every Aquarium Needs
Environmental Diseases of Aquatic Animals in Aquatic Systems
Máy sủi oxy cho bể cá: Cách sử dụng đúng và bảo dưỡng bền lâu

facts.fact: Aeration works by creating a water–air interface where oxygen enters the water and carbon dioxide leaves it.
An air stone mostly adds oxygen by stirring the water surface, which speeds up gas exchange, rather than by the bubbles themselves.
Good aeration comes from either strong, choppy surface agitation or a large number of rising bubbles.
A smooth, glassy water surface gives only about 5% of the aeration of a choppy surface of the same size.
A dissolved oxygen concentration above 5 mg/L is optimal for most finfish, and fish become stressed below 5 mg/L.
Depending on species and exposure time, deaths may occur at 4 mg/L dissolved oxygen or lower.
Aquarium Co-Op gives about 7 to 8 ppm (mg/L) as the ideal oxygen level for freshwater tanks.
Fully saturated water at 78°F holds about 8.25 mg/L of oxygen, and warmer water holds less.
Besides air stones, an air pump can drive a sponge filter, where water is pulled through the sponge and beneficial bacteria live on it, or a moving bed filter.
Fish short of oxygen gather at the surface and gulp air, a behavior called 'piping'.
Piping can also be caused by high nitrite or gill disease, not only by low oxygen.
Other signs of low oxygen are resting on the bottom, poor appetite and rapid gill movement.
In tanks with strong current, fish short of oxygen may swim against the flow with their mouths open.
Oxygen-related deaths often appear early in the morning, when oxygen is lowest, and large fish are usually hit harder than small ones.
Of temperature, salinity and altitude, temperature has the biggest effect on how much oxygen water can hold.
Oxygen drops at night because respiration continues while photosynthesis stops.
Overstocking, overfeeding, cloudy weather and a collapsing algal bloom can all deplete oxygen.
Other causes of low oxygen include high temperature, overcrowding, certain medications or chemicals, and weak surface agitation.
Floating plants that cover the entire surface limit gas exchange.
If oxygen is low, first do a large water change, then look for the cause.

Gas bubble disease from water supersaturated with gas (usually nitrogen) is treated with vigorous aeration to drive off the excess gas, plus fixing the mechanical cause, such as a cavitating pump or an air leak on the intake side.
Signs of gas bubble disease include lethargy, buoyancy problems, bubbles in the gills, fins and eyes, and popeye; fine bubbles may also show on the aquarium glass.
An air system has an air pump, airline tubing and a check valve outside the tank; only the last section of tubing goes into the water, to the air stone or sponge filter.
Tetra Whisper 3i instructions: to prevent electric shock from water siphoning back, use the included check valve or place the pump higher than the water level.
Tetra 77853 manual: if the pump cannot sit above the water level, fit a check valve in the tubing as close to the pump as possible, facing so air flows out and water cannot flow back.
Put the check valve on the air line to stop water flowing back when the pump sits lower than the water surface.
A pump must be strong enough to make hundreds of bubbles per second for an air stone to aerate well; small pumps sold cheaply or bundled with kits are described as too weak.
Aeration demand does not grow in step with fish length: a two-inch fish needs eight times the aeration of a one-inch fish.
In one Aquarium Co-Op test, a 40-gallon breeder with a sponge filter had more oxygen than a 55-gallon tank, because the breeder has more surface area.
In the same tests, a powerhead aimed at the surface did better than a venturi-type powerhead, and a circulation pump did not raise oxygen much.
Strong aeration drives CO2 down to around 2–3 ppm, while plants generally do best above 10 ppm, so aeration can work against injected CO2 in planted tanks.
In dry climates, air pumps with air stones can speed up evaporation; choppy surface flow is preferred there.
The pump diaphragm is the part that wears out most often, and replacement diaphragms are sold.
More aeration is generally better at any temperature, because water at 78°F is not necessarily saturated.
Higher oxygen slows the growth of free-floating bacteria and helps keep water clear.
Running aeration at night helps planted and heavily stocked tanks, because oxygen is lowest overnight.
In high-risk periods, usually hot summer weather, the Merck manual suggests checking oxygen weekly in ponds.
During a power cut, Aquarium Co-Op says that after 8 or more hours without power, run oxygen for 1 hour and repeat every 8 hours; heavily stocked tanks or gasping fish may need it every 4 hours.
In a power cut, do not feed the fish, turn off automatic feeders and do not change water for the first 1–2 hours.
A USB air pump can run from a USB power bank or a laptop during a power cut.
Aquarium Co-Op's battery-backup air pump switches on by itself when power fails and runs about 20 hours, or about 40 hours or more in power-save mode (15 seconds on, 15 seconds off).
Hang-on-back and canister filters hold little oxygen during a power cut; unplugging them stops dirty water flushing into the tank when power returns.

In hot weather without power, move the tank somewhere cool and shaded; a battery fan blowing across the surface cools it by evaporation, while floating frozen bottles is not advised because sudden temperature changes stress fish.
After power returns, wait 24 hours before feeding, test ammonia and nitrite, and change water if either reads above 0 ppm.
Vietnamese names: máy sủi / máy sủi oxy / máy sủi khí (air pump), đá sủi or thanh sủi (air stone or bar), dây sủi (airline tubing), van một chiều (check valve), màng bơm (diaphragm).
Rechargeable air pumps (máy sủi tích điện, sủi AC/DC) are sold in Vietnam as backup during power cuts, and are recommended for high-value fish such as arowana and koi.
Air pump brands sold by Vietnamese aquarium shops include Gex, Periha and Atman.
The rule of 12 square inches of surface per inch of fish is a myth, according to aquariumscience.org.
aquariumscience.org says a tank's surface-area-to-depth ratio is meaningless for judging aeration.
